'''Julian Lowell Coolidge''' (September 28, 1873 – March 5, 1954) was an American [[mathematician]], [[historian]], a [[professor]] and chairman of the [[Harvard University]] Mathematics Department.<ref name="mactutor"/>

==Biography==
Born in [[Brookline, Massachusetts]], he graduated from [[Harvard University]]<ref name="mactutor"/> and [[Balliol College, Oxford]].<ref>Balliol College Register, 3rd Edition, p491</ref>

Between 1897 and 1899, Julian Coolidge taught at the [[Groton School]], where one of his students was [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]].<ref name="mactutor"/> He left Groton to accept a teaching position at Harvard and in 1902 was given an assistant professorship, but took two years off to further his education with studies in [[Turin, Italy]]<ref name="mactutor"/> before receiving his [[doctorate]] from the [[University of Bonn]].<ref name="mactutor"/><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id= 30689}}</ref> Julian Coolidge then returned to teach at Harvard where he remained for his entire academic career, interrupted only by a year at the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]] in Paris as an exchange professor.<ref name="mactutor"/>

During [[World War I]], he served with the [[United States Army|U.S. Army's]] Overseas Expeditionary Force in [[France]], rising to the rank of [[Major (United States)|major]]. In 1919, he was awarded a [[Knight]] of [[France]]'s [[Legion of Honor]].<ref name="mactutor">{{cite web|title=Julian Coolidge|website=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]], University of St Andrews|first1=John J.|last1=O'Connor|first2=Edmund F.|last2=Robertson|language=en|url= https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Coolidge/|access-date=9 September 2021|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210909010902/https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Coolidge/|archive-date=9 September 2021}}</ref>

Coolidge returned to teach at Harvard where he was awarded a full professorship. In 1927 he was appointed chairman of the Mathematics Department at Harvard,<ref name="mactutor"/> a position he held until his retirement in 1940. A Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref>{{citation|title=The Early History of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences|pages=3–23|journal=Bulletin of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences|volume=24|issue=4|year=1971|doi=10.2307/3823172|jstor=3823172}}.</ref> Coolidge served as president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] and vice-president of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="mactutor"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/coolidge.html |title=MAA presidents: Julian Lowell Coolidge |access-date=2013-02-06 |archive-date=2013-01-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130126123656/http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/coolidge.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> He authored several books on mathematics and on the [[history of mathematics]].
He was Master of Lowell House (one of Harvard's undergraduate residences) from 1930 to 1940.{{refn|https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1954/3/6/first-lowell-housemaster-julian-coolidge-dies/}}

Coolidge died in 1954 in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]], aged 80.<ref name="mactutor"/>

*J. L. Coolidge (1909) [https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26373 ''The elements of non-Euclidean geometry''], [[Oxford University Press]].
*J. L. Coolidge (1916) ''[[A Treatise on the Circle and the Sphere]]'', [[Oxford University Press]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=White, H. S.|authorlink=Henry Seely White|title=Circle and Sphere Geometry|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1919|volume=25|issue=10|pages=464–467|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1919-25-10/S0002-9904-1919-03230-3/|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1919-03230-3|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*J. L. Coolidge (1924) ''The geometry of the complex domain'', [[The Clarendon Press]].
*J. L. Coolidge (1925) ''An introduction to mathematical probability'', [[Oxford University Press]].
*J. L. Coolidge (1931) ''A Treatise on Algebraic Plane Curves'', [[Oxford University Press]] ([[Dover Publications]] 2004).
*J. L. Coolidge (1940) ''A history of geometrical methods'',<ref>{{cite journal|author=Snyder, Virgil|authorlink=Virgil Snyder|title=Review: J. L. Coolidge, ''A History of Geometrical Methods''|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1941|volume=47|issue=1|pages=20–22|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183503405|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1941-07368-4|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Oxford University Press]] ([[Dover Publications]] 2003).
*J. L. Coolidge (1945) ''History of the conic sections and quadric surfaces'', [[The Clarendon Press]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Blumenthal, Leonard M.|title=Review: J. L. Coolidge, ''A history of the conic sections and quadrics''|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1947|volume=53|issue=1, Part 1|page=36|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183510301|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1947-08730-9|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*J. L. Coolidge (1949) [https://archive.org/details/mathematicsofgre010690mbp ''The Mathematics Of Great Amateurs''], [[Oxford University Press]] ([[Dover Publications]] 1963).
